paragraphs.text: Seaweed has been eaten in parts of East Asia for thousands of years, but it is only recently that it has become popular in Europe and North America. Supermarkets now sell seaweed snacks, and some chefs use it in place of salt.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Nutritionists point out that many types of seaweed are rich in iodine, which the body needs to produce certain hormones. However, eating large amounts of some varieties can provide far more iodine than is healthy.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Seaweed farming has environmental benefits. It needs no fresh water or fertiliser, and the growing plants absorb carbon dioxide from the sea. Some farms are placed near fish farms, where the seaweed takes up waste nutrients from the fish.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The industry faces challenges. Storms can destroy farms, and seaweed must be dried or processed quickly after harvest, which requires energy. In some regions, local fishermen have objected to farms that occupy traditional fishing areas.
paragraphs.label: D
